assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength lattice proposal and realized with strontium and ytterbium at the 1e-18 level, redefined what can be measured and how accurately. Impact spans timekeeping, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the planned redefinition of the second. From a laser-spectroscopy standpoint this is a clean, concrete instrumentation breakthrough.
assessment.attribution: Katori originated the magic-wavelength lattice idea and early Sr demonstrations; Ye's group drove the precision, coherence and systematic-uncertainty record and the link to frequency combs. Two names give a fair, compact configuration. Other groups (e.g. at NIST and PTB) contributed, but the supplied credit supports this pair; I am relying on memory for the finer attribution history.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs reproduce 1e-18-class performance, and the physics is stable. Recognition is timely, since the redefinition of the second is under discussion; the comb was recognized in 2005 and ion-trap clocks in 2012, which does not preclude this.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier clock-related prizes (Hall and Hansch in 2005, Wineland in 2012) may be seen as incremental by some members.
Whether Ye's contribution is better framed as the clock or as the comb-clock integration is a judgment I cannot verify here.
The formal redefinition of the second has not yet occurred, so maturity of impact is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong light-matter coupling controllable on a chip and is the architecture behind transmon-based quantum processors, dispersive readout and microwave quantum optics. It is an experimental platform of broad, durable impact, and its quantum-optics core is close to my own field.
assessment.attribution: Blais supplied the theory proposal (with Girvin and colleagues), Wallraff and Schoelkopf the first strong-coupling experiments and the transmon and readout developments. The three-name set is plausible, but Girvin, Devoret and others are not in the supplied credit, which leaves an allocation question.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories and underpins a large industry effort. The 2025 prize recognized superconducting-circuit quantum effects, which may make the committee cautious about returning so soon to a closely related area.
uncertainties: Proximity to the recent 2025 superconducting-circuit award may weigh against timing.
Credit excludes some key figures such as Girvin and Devoret, so fairness of the three-person configuration is uncertain.
I cannot independently check the exact priority of the transmon versus the coupling experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposals for trapped-ion quantum gates and the later cold-atom quantum simulation program provided the conceptual foundation of atomic quantum information. The ideas are original, clear and very influential, and they connect directly to experimental AMO practice.
assessment.attribution: The two-name credit is natural and well defined; their joint proposals are widely seen as decisive. Experimental realization belongs to others (Wineland, Blatt and colleagues), which is outside this candidate.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed over decades in ions, neutral atoms and Rydberg systems. Recognition is timely and no longer premature, though the committee may prefer to pair theory with experiment.
uncertainties: The theory-only configuration may be considered incomplete without experimental pioneers such as Blatt.
Overlap with other ballot entries involving the same two theorists complicates how the committee spreads credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the Mott insulator transition to quantum gas microscopes, created a controllable platform for many-body quantum simulation. The work is original, conceptually clear and has been influential across condensed-matter and AMO physics.
assessment.attribution: Bloch and Greiner carried out the decisive experiments (Mott transition, microscopy), and Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) proposed the lattice Bose-Hubbard realization. Others, such as Cirac, Hansch and Kasevich, also contributed and the allocation is not fully clear.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many groups, and the platform is mature. Recognition is timely. Some of the scientific payoff, such as quantum advantage for simulation, is still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the foundations candidate and with Zoller's role in other entries; whether Bloch alone or a trio is best is uncertain.
Exact priority among the Munich, Harvard and other contributions is from memory and not verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays with optical-tweezer assembly provide a scalable, high-fidelity platform for quantum simulation and computing, including quantum phase transitions and neutral-atom gates. The impact is large and rapidly growing; the technique draws on laser cooling and coherent control familiar from my field.
assessment.attribution: Lukin's group and Browaeys's group built the key array and simulation experiments, and Saffman contributed the Rydberg blockade gate proposal and experiments. Others (Bernien, Endres, Weiss, Jaksch) matter, so the three-person assignment is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several groups and companies, but the field is still moving quickly and the interpretation of which achievements are most lasting is not settled. Possibly somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Fast-moving field with no settled consensus on decisive contributions.
Credit allocation with Jaksch, Endres, Bernien and others is unresolved.
Long-term impact on computing is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optically addressable spins in diamond and related solids enabled single-spin readout at room temperature, nanoscale quantum sensing and quantum network nodes. This links laser spectroscopy of solid-state defects to metrology and aligns with the idea that progress is limited by what we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the first single-NV optical detection and coherent control; Awschalom extended coherent control and defect-spin platforms across materials. Lukin and others are also credited in the list, so fair selection among four names is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely used in sensing and networks. The field is broad, so identifying one discovery is somewhat harder, but timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: The compound nature (single-spin detection, sensing, networks, other materials) may need different recognition.
Choosing three of four credited names leaves an allocation question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Solid-state femtosecond lasers, including Ti:sapphire, Kerr-lens mode locking and SESAMs, replaced dye lasers and enabled practical ultrafast science. Their impact on spectroscopy and metrology is large and the invention is clear.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed Ti:sapphire as a laser medium, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode locking, and Keller invented the SESAM. This is a reasonable three-way split, although Spence and others in the Kerr-lens story are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and ubiquitous. Concern is that ultrafast optics was recognized in 2018 (chirped pulse amplification) and 2023 (attosecond pulses), so the committee may see this as already largely honored.
uncertainties: Prior ultrafast-laser prizes may make this seem less novel.
Credit for Kerr-lens mode locking among Sibbett and colleagues is partly uncertain from my memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum control of mechanical motion, including ground-state cooling, sideband cooling and mechanical quantum states, tests quantum mechanics with macroscopic objects and enables ultrasensitive measurement. The measurement-limit perspective gives it strong appeal, though the exact decisive discovery is diffuse.
assessment.attribution: Cleland demonstrated a mechanical resonator in its quantum ground state, Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer developed cavity optomechanics and ground-state cooling. Others (Schwab, Teufel, Painter, Lehnert) also made key contributions, so the three-name set is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Replicated across several platforms, but applications are still emerging and the committee may judge it somewhat early. Some overlap with the 2025 prize theme of macroscopic quantum behavior.
uncertainties: Credit is spread among many groups and platforms.
Overlap with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits.
Practical and scientific impact is not yet fully demonstrated.
